sections.title: Section A — Units I to IV (compulsory)
Section B1 — Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
Section B2 — Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Past adjustments — interest on drawings omitted
questions.question: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 and their capitals are fixed. After the accounts were closed, it was found that interest on drawings at 6% p.a. had not been charged. A's drawings were ₹40,000 and B's were ₹20,000, both spread evenly over the year. The single adjusting entry will be:
options: A) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹120; To B's Current A/c ₹120
B) B's Current A/c Dr. ₹120; To A's Current A/c ₹120
C) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹1,200; To B's Current A/c ₹1,200
D) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹1,080; To B's Current A/c ₹1,080
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A's Current A/c Dr. ₹120; To B's Current A/c ₹120
Given: Drawings spread evenly → average period 6 months; rate 6% p.a.; profit ratio 3 : 2.
Step 1: Interest to be charged: A = ₹40,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,200; B = ₹20,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹600 (total ₹1,800)
Step 2: The ₹1,800 would have increased divisible profit, so it is credited back in 3 : 2: A ₹1,080; B ₹720
Step 3: Net: A = −₹1,200 + ₹1,080 = −₹120 (debit); B = −₹600 + ₹720 = +₹120 (credit)
Common mistake: Reversing the direction gives (B). Using only A's interest gives (C). Using only A's profit share gives (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares for consideration other than cash — purchase of business
questions.question: Raj Ltd. purchased the business of Gupta Bros., taking over assets of ₹5,00,000 and liabilities of ₹1,00,000, for a purchase consideration of ₹4,40,000. It paid ₹40,000 in cash and the balance by issuing equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of 25%. The number of shares issued and the goodwill/capital reserve arising are:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 32,000 shares; Goodwill ₹40,000
Given: Net assets = ₹5,00,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000; purchase consideration ₹4,40,000; cash ₹40,000; issue price ₹10 + 25% = ₹12.50.
Step 1: PC > net assets → Goodwill = ₹4,40,000 − ₹4,00,000 = ₹40,000 (if PC were lower, the difference would be Capital Reserve)
Step 2: Paid in shares = ₹4,40,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹4,00,000
Step 3: Number of shares = ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹12.50 = 32,000 (Share Capital ₹3,20,000 + Securities Premium ₹80,000)
Common mistake: Reversing goodwill and capital reserve gives (A). Dividing by the face value of ₹10 gives 40,000 shares (C). Ignoring the cash paid gives 35,200 shares (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of dissolution of a firm
questions.question: Dissolution of a partnership FIRM means:
options: A) A change in the profit-sharing ratio of the existing partners
B) The admission of a new partner
C) Closure of the business, with the firm ceasing to exist
D) The retirement of a partner while the others continue the business
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Closure of the business, with the firm ceasing to exist
Why: Under Section 39 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, dissolution of a firm means dissolving the partnership between ALL the partners. The business is closed, assets are realised, liabilities are paid and the firm comes to an end.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) only change the relationship among partners — that is dissolution (reconstitution) of the PARTNERSHIP, and the firm continues.
Key point: Dissolution of partnership → firm continues; dissolution of firm → firm ends.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question: Interest on debentures is:
options: B) Payable only when the company earns a profit
D) A charge against profit, payable whether or not there is a profit
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A charge against profit, payable whether or not there is a profit
Why: Debenture holders are creditors entitled to a fixed rate of interest. It is debited to the Statement of Profit and Loss under Finance costs, even in a loss year.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) describe dividend on shares, which is an appropriation and depends on profit.
(C) Interest is a revenue expense, not capital expenditure.
Key point: Interest on debentures = finance cost (charge); dividend = appropriation.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — revaluation of assets and liabilities
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 2 : 1 : 1. C retires. On his retirement: Building of ₹2,50,000 is appreciated by 20%; Stock of ₹80,000 is reduced by 10%; and a provision for doubtful debts at 5% is to be created on debtors of ₹60,000. C's share of profit or loss on revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Profit ₹9,750
Given: Building +20% of ₹2,50,000; stock −10% of ₹80,000; new provision 5% of ₹60,000.
Step 1: Gain on building = ₹50,000
Step 2: Losses = stock ₹8,000 + provision ₹3,000 = ₹11,000
Step 3: Revaluation profit = ₹50,000 − ₹11,000 = ₹39,000, shared by ALL partners (including C) in the old ratio 2 : 1 : 1
Step 4: C's share = ₹39,000 × 1/4 = ₹9,750 (credited to C's Capital A/c)
Common mistake: ₹39,000 (B) is the firm's total profit. ₹19,500 (C) is A's share. Sharing equally among three gives ₹13,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital when profit is insufficient
questions.question: A and B have capitals of ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000. The deed provides interest on capital at 10% p.a. as an appropriation of profit. The firm's profit before interest on capital is only ₹40,000. The amount allowed to A as interest on capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹24,000
Given: Interest due A ₹30,000, B ₹20,000 (total ₹50,000); available profit only ₹40,000.
Why: Interest on capital is an appropriation, so it cannot exceed the profit available. The whole profit is distributed in the ratio of the interest due (₹30,000 : ₹20,000 = 3 : 2).
Step 1: A = ₹40,000 × 3/5 = ₹24,000; B = ₹40,000 × 2/5 = ₹16,000
Common mistake: Allowing full interest gives ₹30,000 (A), which creates a loss that is not permitted. Splitting the profit equally gives ₹20,000 (B). ₹16,000 (D) is B's amount.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Provisions applicable in the absence of a partnership deed
questions.question:
Which of the following rules apply when partners have NOT made a partnership deed?
(A) No partner is entitled to a salary.
(B) Interest on capital is allowed at 6% p.a.
(C) No interest is charged on drawings.
(D) Profits and losses are shared equally.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: Section 13 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 applies when there is no deed: no salary or other remuneration to partners (A), no interest on drawings (C), and equal sharing of profits and losses (D).
Why not the others: Statement (B) is false. No interest on capital is allowed without an agreement; 6% p.a. applies only to a partner's LOAN. Options (A), (C) and (D) all include statement (B).
Key point: No deed → 6% p.a. on loans only; nothing on capital or drawings; no salary; equal shares.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A company cannot allot shares to applicants unless it has received the minimum subscription stated in its prospectus.
Reason (R): Minimum subscription ensures that the company raises enough funds to carry out the purposes for which the issue is made.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Under Section 39 of the Companies Act, 2013 (and SEBI's 90% requirement for public issues), allotment can be made only if the minimum subscription is received; otherwise the application money must be refunded. The rule exists precisely so that a company does not start a project without the funds needed for it — which is what the Reason states.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason is the purpose behind the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Minimum subscription not received → no allotment → refund application money.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Term)
(A) Sacrificing ratio
(B) Gaining ratio
(C) Hidden goodwill
(D) Super profit

List-II (Meaning)
(I) Excess of average profit over normal profit
(II) Ratio in which old partners give up their share in favour of a new partner
(III) Ratio in which continuing partners acquire the share of a retiring partner
(IV) Goodwill inferred from the capital brought in by a new partner

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) Sacrificing ratio is the ratio in which old partners surrender their share to an incoming partner → (II).
(B) Gaining ratio is the ratio in which continuing partners take over the share of a retiring or deceased partner → (III).
(C) Hidden goodwill is the goodwill implied by the new partner's capital contribution compared with the total capital → (IV).
(D) Super profit = average profit − normal profit → (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps sacrificing and gaining ratios; (B) swaps hidden goodwill and super profit; (C) mismatches three of the pairs.
Key point: Admission → sacrificing ratio; retirement/death → gaining ratio.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question: A debenture holder is a ____ of the company.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Creditor
Why: A debenture is an acknowledgement of a debt taken by the company. The holder has lent money and receives a fixed interest whether or not the company earns a profit.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) Shareholders are the owners and members. (C) A debtor owes money TO the company.
Key point: Shareholder = owner (dividend); debenture holder = creditor (interest).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question: A company is registered with 10,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each. It issued 6,00,000 shares, of which 5,50,000 were subscribed. ₹8 per share has been called up. Calls in arrears amount to ₹20,000. The company's paid-up capital is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹43,80,000
Given: Subscribed 5,50,000 shares; called up ₹8 per share; calls in arrears ₹20,000.
Step 1: Called-up capital = 5,50,000 × ₹8 = ₹44,00,000
Step 2: Paid-up capital = Called-up − Calls in arrears = ₹44,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹43,80,000
Common mistake: ₹60,00,000 (A) is the issued capital at face value. ₹44,00,000 (B) is the called-up capital. ₹55,00,000 (C) is the subscribed capital at face value.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question: A firm's average profit is ₹1,10,000 and its capital employed is ₹8,00,000. The normal rate of return is 12%. Goodwill is to be valued at three years' purchase of super profit. The value of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹42,000
Given: Average profit ₹1,10,000; capital employed ₹8,00,000; normal rate 12%; 3 years' purchase.
Step 1: Normal profit = ₹8,00,000 × 12% = ₹96,000
Step 2: Super profit = ₹1,10,000 − ₹96,000 = ₹14,000
Step 3: Goodwill = ₹14,000 × 3 = ₹42,000
Common mistake: Multiplying the average profit by 3 gives ₹3,30,000 (A). ₹14,000 (C) is the super profit before multiplying. Multiplying the normal profit by 3 gives ₹2,88,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of debentures at a premium, redeemable at a premium
questions.question: A company issued 1,000, 9% debentures of ₹100 each at a premium of 5%, redeemable at a premium of 10% after four years. The amount debited to the Loss on Issue of Debentures Account at the time of issue is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹10,000
Given: Premium on issue 5% (₹5 per debenture); premium on redemption 10% (₹10 per debenture).
Entry: Bank A/c Dr. ₹1,05,000; Loss on Issue of Debentures A/c Dr. ₹10,000; To 9% Debentures A/c ₹1,00,000; To Securities Premium A/c ₹5,000; To Premium on Redemption of Debentures A/c ₹10,000
Step 1: Loss on issue = premium payable on redemption = 1,000 × ₹10 = ₹10,000
Step 2: The ₹5,000 premium received is credited separately to Securities Premium A/c. It is not netted against the loss.
Common mistake: Taking the premium on issue gives ₹5,000 (A). Adding both premiums gives ₹15,000 (B). Netting the two (₹10,000 − ₹5,000) or assuming no loss when issued at a premium leads to (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Writing off loss on issue of debentures
questions.question: At the end of the year in which debentures were issued, the Loss on Issue of Debentures Account shows a balance of ₹60,000 and the Securities Premium Account has a balance of ₹25,000. Following the treatment prescribed in NCERT, the amount to be written off to the Statement of Profit and Loss is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹35,000
Given: Loss on issue ₹60,000; Securities Premium available ₹25,000.
Why: Section 52 permits Securities Premium to be used for writing off discount or loss on issue of debentures. NCERT therefore writes the loss off first against Securities Premium, and charges any balance to the Statement of Profit and Loss (as a finance cost) in the year of issue.
Step 1: Written off against Securities Premium = ₹25,000
Step 2: Charged to Statement of P&L = ₹60,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹35,000
Common mistake: Charging the whole loss to P&L gives ₹60,000 (B). ₹25,000 (C) is the part met from Securities Premium. Spreading over five years gives ₹12,000 (D), which is not the treatment prescribed now.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.question: As per the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014, the maximum number of partners a partnership firm can have is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 50
Why: Section 464 of the Companies Act, 2013 lets the government prescribe the maximum number of partners in a firm. Rule 10 of the Companies (Miscellaneous) Rules, 2014 fixes it at 50. An association of more than 50 persons carrying on business for profit must register as a company.
Why not the others:
(A) 10 was the old limit for a banking business under the Companies Act, 1956.
(B) 20 was the old limit for other businesses under the 1956 Act.
(D) 100 is not a limit prescribed for partnership firms.
Key point: Minimum 2 partners, maximum 50.

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Creditors accepting an asset in settlement
questions.question: On dissolution, creditors of ₹40,000 accepted the firm's stock (book value ₹35,000), which had already been transferred to the Realisation Account, in full settlement of their claim. The entry required for this settlement is:
options: A) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹40,000; To Cash A/c ₹40,000
B) Creditors A/c Dr. ₹40,000; To Stock A/c ₹35,000 and To Realisation A/c ₹5,000
D) Realisation A/c Dr. ₹35,000; To Stock A/c ₹35,000
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) No entry is required
Why: Both the stock (debit side) and the creditors (credit side) are already in the Realisation Account. When creditors take the stock in full settlement, no cash moves, and both items stay in the Realisation Account. The difference (₹40,000 − ₹35,000 = ₹5,000) automatically shows up as part of the realisation profit.
Why not the others:
(A) No cash was paid.
(B) and (D) The Stock and Creditors accounts were already closed by transfer to the Realisation Account.
Key point: Asset given to a creditor in full settlement → no entry. Only extra cash paid (or received) is recorded.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about calls in advance:
(A) Calls in advance is a liability of the company until the call is made.
(B) Under Table F, interest at a rate not exceeding 12% p.a. may be paid on calls in advance.
(C) Calls in advance forms part of the company's paid-up share capital.
(D) Calls in advance is shown under 'Other current liabilities' in the balance sheet.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why:
(A) True — money received before the call is made is owed back to the shareholder until the call is due.
(B) True — Table F allows interest of up to 12% p.a. on calls in advance (on calls in arrears the rate is up to 10% p.a.).
(D) True — Schedule III shows it under Other current liabilities.
(C) False — it is not part of share capital until the call is actually made.
Why not the others: Options (B), (C) and (D) all include the false statement (C).
Key point: Calls in advance = liability (12% interest); calls in arrears = deducted from called-up capital (10% interest).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Issue of shares at a premium — under-subscription
questions.question: A company issued 20,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share, the premium being payable with the allotment money. Applications were received for 18,000 shares and all were allotted. A shareholder holding 500 shares failed to pay the allotment money. The amount credited to the Securities Premium Account at the time of allotment is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹36,000
Given: 18,000 shares actually allotted (under-subscription); premium ₹2 per share due with allotment.
Why: The premium is credited when the allotment money becomes DUE, on all shares allotted, whether or not it is later paid. Non-payment is shown as calls in arrears. If those shares are later forfeited, Securities Premium is debited by the unpaid premium (₹1,000) at that time.
Step 1: Securities Premium = 18,000 × ₹2 = ₹36,000
Common mistake: Using the 20,000 shares offered gives ₹40,000 (A). Excluding the defaulter's 500 shares gives ₹35,000 (B). ₹1,000 (D) is the defaulter's unpaid premium.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Interest on a partner's loan to the firm is payable even when the firm suffers a loss.
Reason (R): Interest on a partner's loan is a charge against profit and not an appropriation of profit.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: A partner's loan is like any outside borrowing. Its interest (6% p.a. unless agreed otherwise) is debited to the Profit and Loss Account as a charge. Because charges must be paid whether the firm earns a profit or not, interest on a loan is payable even in a year of loss — which is exactly why the Assertion holds.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason does explain the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Charge (loan interest, rent to partner) → always paid; appropriation (interest on capital, salary) → only out of profit.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on capital — additional capital introduced
questions.question: On 1 April 2025, A's capital was ₹2,00,000. He introduced additional capital of ₹50,000 on 1 October 2025. Interest on capital is allowed at 10% p.a. The books are closed on 31 March 2026. Interest on A's capital will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹22,500
Given: Opening capital ₹2,00,000 for 12 months; additional ₹50,000 from 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026 (6 months); rate 10% p.a.
Step 1: Interest on opening capital = ₹2,00,000 × 10% = ₹20,000
Step 2: Interest on additional capital = ₹50,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹2,500
Step 3: Total = ₹20,000 + ₹2,500 = ₹22,500
Common mistake: Charging the full year on ₹2,50,000 gives ₹25,000 (B); ignoring the additional capital gives ₹20,000 (C); counting only 3 months on the additional capital gives ₹21,250 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death of a partner — amount payable to executors
questions.question: On the death of partner D, the following were ascertained: D's capital ₹80,000; his share of goodwill ₹30,000; his share of profit up to the date of death ₹6,000; interest on his capital up to the date of death ₹2,000; and his drawings up to the date of death ₹10,000. The amount transferred to D's Executor's Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹1,08,000
Given: Credits — capital ₹80,000, goodwill ₹30,000, profit ₹6,000, interest on capital ₹2,000. Debit — drawings ₹10,000.
Step 1: Total credits = 80,000 + 30,000 + 6,000 + 2,000 = ₹1,18,000
Step 2: Less drawings = ₹10,000
Step 3: Balance transferred to D's Executor's A/c = ₹1,08,000
Common mistake: Adding the drawings instead of deducting them gives ₹1,28,000 (B). Ignoring the drawings gives ₹1,18,000 (C). Leaving out goodwill gives ₹78,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Retirement — adjustment of goodwill in gaining ratio
questions.question: A, B and C share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. C retires and the firm's goodwill is valued at ₹1,20,000. A and B decide to share future profits in the ratio 3 : 2. The amount debited to A's Capital Account for C's share of goodwill will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹12,000
Given: Old ratio 3 : 2 : 1; new ratio of A and B 3 : 2; goodwill ₹1,20,000.
Step 1: C's share of goodwill = ₹1,20,000 × 1/6 = ₹20,000
Step 2: Gaining ratio: A = 3/5 − 3/6 = 3/30; B = 2/5 − 2/6 = 2/30 → 3 : 2
Step 3: A's Capital A/c Dr. = ₹20,000 × 3/5 = ₹12,000 (B's ₹8,000); C's Capital A/c Cr. ₹20,000
Common mistake: Sharing C's goodwill equally gives ₹10,000 (A). ₹20,000 (B) is C's whole share. ₹60,000 (D) is A's share of the firm's total goodwill, which is never recorded under AS-26.

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.question: Authorised capital of a company is:
options: A) The amount actually received from shareholders
B) The maximum share capital the company is authorised to raise, as stated in its Memorandum of Association
C) The part of issued capital subscribed by the public
D) The part of subscribed capital called up by the company
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The maximum share capital the company is authorised to raise, as stated in its Memorandum of Association
Why: Authorised (registered or nominal) capital is the upper limit set in the capital clause of the Memorandum. The company cannot issue shares beyond it unless the Memorandum is altered.
Why not the others:
(A) This describes paid-up capital.
(C) This describes subscribed capital.
(D) This describes called-up capital.
Key point: Authorised ≥ Issued ≥ Subscribed ≥ Called-up ≥ Paid-up.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Interest on drawings — unequal amounts on different dates
questions.question: During the year ended 31 March 2026, a partner withdrew ₹10,000 on 1 July 2025, ₹6,000 on 1 October 2025 and ₹4,000 on 1 January 2026. Interest on drawings is charged at 12% p.a. The interest on drawings will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹1,380
Given: Drawings on different dates — interest is charged from each date to 31 March 2026.
Step 1: ₹10,000 from 1 July → 9 months: ₹10,000 × 12% × 9/12 = ₹900
Step 2: ₹6,000 from 1 October → 6 months: ₹6,000 × 12% × 6/12 = ₹360
Step 3: ₹4,000 from 1 January → 3 months: ₹4,000 × 12% × 3/12 = ₹120
Step 4: Total interest = ₹900 + ₹360 + ₹120 = ₹1,380
Common mistake: Charging a full year on ₹20,000 gives ₹2,400 (A). Using an average of 6 months for all the drawings gives ₹1,200 (B). Counting the months inclusively (10, 7 and 4) gives ₹1,580 (C).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about realisation expenses on dissolution of a firm:
(A) Expenses paid by the firm are debited to the Realisation Account.
(B) Expenses paid by a partner on behalf of the firm are debited to the Realisation Account and credited to that partner's Capital Account.
(C) When a partner has agreed to bear the expenses and pays them himself, no entry is passed in the firm's books.
(D) When the firm pays expenses that a partner has agreed to bear, the Realisation Account is debited.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why:
(A) True — the firm's own expenses reduce the realisation profit.
(B) True — the partner has paid a firm expense, so the firm owes him that amount.
(C) True — the expense is neither the firm's cost nor paid by the firm, so nothing is recorded.
(D) False — if the firm pays an expense that a partner must bear, it is recovered from that partner: Partner's Capital A/c Dr.; To Cash A/c. The Realisation Account is not debited.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (C) all include the false statement (D).
Key point: Ask two questions — whose expense is it, and who paid it?

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Unrecorded assets and liabilities on dissolution
questions.question: On the dissolution of a firm, an unrecorded computer valued at ₹8,000 is taken over by partner P, and an unrecorded liability of ₹3,000 is paid in cash. The net effect of these two items on the Realisation Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Profit of ₹5,000
Given: Unrecorded asset taken over by P at ₹8,000; unrecorded liability paid ₹3,000.
Step 1: Asset taken over → P's Capital A/c Dr. ₹8,000; To Realisation A/c ₹8,000 (a gain)
Step 2: Unrecorded liability paid → Realisation A/c Dr. ₹3,000; To Cash A/c ₹3,000 (a loss)
Step 3: Net effect = ₹8,000 − ₹3,000 = profit of ₹5,000
Common mistake: Reversing the effects gives a loss of ₹5,000 (A). Treating the liability as a gain gives ₹11,000 (C). Ignoring the liability gives ₹8,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit III: Dissolution of Partnership Firm
questions.question: On dissolution, partner P's capital account shows a credit balance of ₹50,000. His share of General Reserve is ₹6,000 and his share of loss on realisation is ₹9,000. He took over an asset at ₹12,000. His loan of ₹10,000 to the firm was settled separately. The amount of cash finally paid to P on his capital account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹35,000
Given: Capital ₹50,000 (Cr.); reserve +₹6,000; realisation loss −₹9,000; asset taken over −₹12,000; loan settled separately.
Step 1: Credits = ₹50,000 + ₹6,000 = ₹56,000
Step 2: Debits = ₹9,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹21,000
Step 3: Cash paid to P = ₹56,000 − ₹21,000 = ₹35,000
Note: Under Section 48 the loan is paid before capital, through P's Loan A/c — it is not part of the capital account.
Common mistake: Adding the ₹10,000 loan gives ₹45,000 (B). Treating the realisation loss as a credit gives ₹53,000 (C). Forgetting the asset taken over gives ₹47,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Debentures — terms of issue and redemption
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Terms of issue of debentures)
(A) Issued at par, redeemable at a premium
(B) Issued at a discount, redeemable at par
(C) Issued at a premium, redeemable at par
(D) Issued at a discount, redeemable at a premium

List-II (Accounting effect at the time of issue)
(I) Securities Premium is credited; no loss on issue
(II) Loss on issue = discount on issue + premium on redemption
(III) Loss on issue = premium on redemption only
(IV) Discount on issue is debited; no premium on redemption

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why:
(A) Par issue + premium on redemption → the only loss is the redemption premium → (III).
(B) Discount issue + par redemption → only the discount is debited → (IV).
(C) Premium issue + par redemption → Securities Premium is credited and there is no loss → (I).
(D) Discount issue + premium redemption → loss = discount + redemption premium → (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps (A) and (D); (C) swaps (B) and (C); (D) swaps (A) and (B).
Key point: Redemption premium is a loss on issue (credited to Premium on Redemption A/c); issue premium is a gain (credited to Securities Premium A/c).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Goodwill — steps in the super profit method
questions.question:
The average profit of a firm is known. Arrange the following steps for valuing goodwill by the super profit method in the correct order:
(A) Calculate the normal profit
(B) Calculate the super profit
(C) Multiply the super profit by the number of years' purchase
(D) Calculate the capital employed
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D), (A), (B), (C)
Why: Each step needs the result of the one before it.
1. Capital employed (D) is needed to find the normal profit.
2. Normal profit = Capital employed × Normal rate of return (A).
3. Super profit = Average profit − Normal profit (B).
4. Goodwill = Super profit × Number of years' purchase (C).
Why not the others: (A) and (C) find normal profit before capital employed. (B) finds super profit before normal profit.
Key point: Capital employed → normal profit → super profit → goodwill.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question: Goodwill of a business is classified as a(n):
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Intangible asset
Why: Goodwill is the value of a firm's reputation, which lets it earn more than normal profits. It cannot be seen or touched, but it has real value and can be sold with the business. So it is an intangible asset (shown under Intangible assets in Schedule III).
Why not the others:
(A) Fictitious assets (such as preliminary expenses written off over time) have no realisable value, whereas goodwill does.
(B) Current assets are converted into cash within a year.
(C) Tangible assets have physical existence.
Key point: Goodwill → intangible, not fictitious.

questions.topic: Unit I: Accounting for Partnership
questions.sub_topic: Guarantee of profit — deficiency borne by two partners
questions.question: P, Q and R share profits in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1. R is guaranteed a minimum profit of ₹20,000; any deficiency is to be borne by P and Q in their mutual ratio. The firm's profit is ₹96,000. Q's share of profit will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹30,400
Given: Ratio 3 : 2 : 1; profit ₹96,000; R guaranteed ₹20,000; deficiency borne by P and Q in 3 : 2.
Step 1: R's share = ₹96,000 × 1/6 = ₹16,000; deficiency = ₹20,000 − ₹16,000 = ₹4,000
Step 2: P bears 3/5 × ₹4,000 = ₹2,400; Q bears 2/5 × ₹4,000 = ₹1,600
Step 3: Q's share = ₹96,000 × 2/6 − ₹1,600 = ₹32,000 − ₹1,600 = ₹30,400
Common mistake: Ignoring the guarantee gives ₹32,000 (A). Sharing the deficiency equally gives ₹30,000 (C). Charging Q with P's portion of ₹2,400 gives ₹29,600 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Which of the following factors increase the goodwill of a firm?
(A) Favourable location of the business
(B) Efficient and stable management
(C) Special advantages such as an import licence or assured supply of scarce raw material
(D) Frequent changes in the management team
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: NCERT lists the factors affecting goodwill as nature of business, location, efficiency of management, market situation, special advantages and so on. A good location (A), efficient and stable management (B) and special advantages (C) all help the firm earn above-normal profits, so they raise goodwill.
Why not the others: (D) Frequent changes in management disturb business continuity and reduce goodwill, so any option containing (D) is wrong.
Key point: Anything that helps earn super profits consistently increases goodwill.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.sub_topic: Death of a partner — share of goodwill
questions.question: D, a partner with a 1/4th share of profits, died. Goodwill is to be valued at two years' purchase of the average profit of the last three years, which were ₹60,000, ₹80,000 and ₹1,00,000. D's share of goodwill is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹40,000
Given: Profits ₹60,000, ₹80,000, ₹1,00,000; 2 years' purchase; D's share 1/4.
Step 1: Average profit = ₹2,40,000 ÷ 3 = ₹80,000
Step 2: Firm's goodwill = ₹80,000 × 2 = ₹1,60,000
Step 3: D's share = ₹1,60,000 × 1/4 = ₹40,000 (credited to D's Capital A/c, debited to the remaining partners in their gaining ratio)
Common mistake: ₹1,60,000 (A) is the firm's goodwill. Taking one year's purchase gives ₹20,000 (C). Applying 1/4 to the total three-year profit gives ₹60,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Re-issue of part of the forfeited shares
questions.question: 500 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called up, were forfeited for non-payment; ₹4 per share had been received on them. Of these, 300 shares were re-issued at ₹7 per share as fully paid. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹300
Given: Forfeited amount ₹4 per share on 500 shares (₹2,000 in Share Forfeiture A/c); 300 shares re-issued at a discount of ₹3 per share.
Step 1: Forfeited amount relating to the re-issued shares = 300 × ₹4 = ₹1,200
Step 2: Discount on re-issue = 300 × ₹3 = ₹900
Step 3: Capital Reserve = ₹1,200 − ₹900 = ₹300. The remaining ₹800 on the 200 shares not yet re-issued stays in Share Forfeiture A/c.
Common mistake: Transferring the gross forfeited amount on 300 shares gives ₹1,200 (A). ₹2,000 (C) is the forfeited amount on all 500 shares. Deducting the discount from the total forfeiture gives ₹1,100 (D).

questions.topic: Unit IV: Company Accounts — Accounting for Share and Debenture Capital
questions.sub_topic: Share capital — types of shares (preference shares)
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about preference shares:
(A) Preference shareholders receive dividend at a fixed rate before any dividend is paid to equity shareholders.
(B) On winding up, preference share capital is repaid before equity share capital.
(C) Preference shareholders normally have voting rights on all matters.
(D) Arrears of dividend on cumulative preference shares are carried forward to later years.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why:
(A) True — preference in dividend at a fixed rate.
(B) True — preference in repayment of capital on winding up.
(D) True — unpaid dividend on cumulative shares accumulates and must be paid before equity dividend.
(C) False — preference shareholders normally vote only on matters directly affecting their rights (or when their dividend is in arrears). Voting on all matters belongs to equity shareholders.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) all include the false statement (C).
Key point: The two preferential rights are dividend first and capital repayment first.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P and Q are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2. On 1 April 2026 they admit R as a new partner, and the new profit-sharing ratio of P, Q and R is 2 : 1 : 1. On that date their balance sheet showed: Capitals — P ₹1,20,000 and Q ₹80,000; General Reserve ₹25,000; Building ₹1,50,000; Stock ₹60,000; Debtors ₹50,000 less Provision for doubtful debts ₹2,000. It was agreed that: (i) Building be appreciated by 10%; (ii) Stock be reduced by ₹6,000; (iii) Provision for doubtful debts be maintained at 5% of debtors; (iv) Outstanding rent of ₹1,500 be recorded; and (v) R brings ₹80,000 as capital and ₹20,000 as premium for goodwill, in cash.

Question: The sacrificing ratio of P and Q is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2 : 3
Given: Old ratio 3 : 2 = 12/20 : 8/20; new ratio 2 : 1 : 1 → P 2/4 = 10/20, Q 1/4 = 5/20.
Step 1: P's sacrifice = 12/20 − 10/20 = 2/20
Step 2: Q's sacrifice = 8/20 − 5/20 = 3/20
Step 3: Sacrificing ratio = 2 : 3
Common mistake: Assuming the old ratio is also the sacrificing ratio gives 3 : 2 (B) — that holds only when the new partner takes his share in the old ratio. 1 : 1 (C) and 2 : 1 (D) compare the new shares instead of the sacrifices.

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P and Q are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2. On 1 April 2026 they admit R as a new partner, and the new profit-sharing ratio of P, Q and R is 2 : 1 : 1. On that date their balance sheet showed: Capitals — P ₹1,20,000 and Q ₹80,000; General Reserve ₹25,000; Building ₹1,50,000; Stock ₹60,000; Debtors ₹50,000 less Provision for doubtful debts ₹2,000. It was agreed that: (i) Building be appreciated by 10%; (ii) Stock be reduced by ₹6,000; (iii) Provision for doubtful debts be maintained at 5% of debtors; (iv) Outstanding rent of ₹1,500 be recorded; and (v) R brings ₹80,000 as capital and ₹20,000 as premium for goodwill, in cash.

Question: The profit or loss on revaluation is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Profit ₹7,000
Step 1: Building +10% of ₹1,50,000 = +₹15,000 (gain)
Step 2: Stock −₹6,000 (loss)
Step 3: Required provision = 5% × ₹50,000 = ₹2,500; existing ₹2,000 → additional ₹500 (loss)
Step 4: Outstanding rent ₹1,500 (loss)
Step 5: Net = ₹15,000 − ₹6,000 − ₹500 − ₹1,500 = profit ₹7,000, shared by P and Q in the old ratio 3 : 2
Common mistake: Ignoring the outstanding rent gives ₹8,500 (A). Charging the full ₹2,500 provision without considering the existing ₹2,000 gives ₹5,000 (B). Ignoring the fall in stock gives ₹13,000 (C).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P and Q are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2. On 1 April 2026 they admit R as a new partner, and the new profit-sharing ratio of P, Q and R is 2 : 1 : 1. On that date their balance sheet showed: Capitals — P ₹1,20,000 and Q ₹80,000; General Reserve ₹25,000; Building ₹1,50,000; Stock ₹60,000; Debtors ₹50,000 less Provision for doubtful debts ₹2,000. It was agreed that: (i) Building be appreciated by 10%; (ii) Stock be reduced by ₹6,000; (iii) Provision for doubtful debts be maintained at 5% of debtors; (iv) Outstanding rent of ₹1,500 be recorded; and (v) R brings ₹80,000 as capital and ₹20,000 as premium for goodwill, in cash.

Question: The amount of goodwill premium credited to Q's Capital Account is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ₹12,000
Given: Premium ₹20,000; sacrificing ratio P : Q = 2 : 3 (see the earlier question in this case).
Step 1: Premium for goodwill is credited to the sacrificing partners in their SACRIFICING ratio
Step 2: Q's share = ₹20,000 × 3/5 = ₹12,000 (P gets ₹8,000)
Common mistake: Using the old ratio 3 : 2 gives Q ₹8,000 (A). Sharing equally gives ₹10,000 (B). Applying Q's new share of 1/4 gives ₹5,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P and Q are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2. On 1 April 2026 they admit R as a new partner, and the new profit-sharing ratio of P, Q and R is 2 : 1 : 1. On that date their balance sheet showed: Capitals — P ₹1,20,000 and Q ₹80,000; General Reserve ₹25,000; Building ₹1,50,000; Stock ₹60,000; Debtors ₹50,000 less Provision for doubtful debts ₹2,000. It was agreed that: (i) Building be appreciated by 10%; (ii) Stock be reduced by ₹6,000; (iii) Provision for doubtful debts be maintained at 5% of debtors; (iv) Outstanding rent of ₹1,500 be recorded; and (v) R brings ₹80,000 as capital and ₹20,000 as premium for goodwill, in cash.

Question: After all the above adjustments, the balance of P's Capital Account will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,47,200
Given: Old ratio 3 : 2; sacrificing ratio 2 : 3; revaluation profit ₹7,000; General Reserve ₹25,000; premium ₹20,000.
Step 1: Opening capital = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: General Reserve (old ratio) = ₹25,000 × 3/5 = +₹15,000
Step 3: Revaluation profit (old ratio) = ₹7,000 × 3/5 = +₹4,200
Step 4: Premium for goodwill (sacrificing ratio) = ₹20,000 × 2/5 = +₹8,000
Step 5: Closing balance = 1,20,000 + 15,000 + 4,200 + 8,000 = ₹1,47,200
Common mistake: Crediting the premium in the old ratio (₹12,000) gives ₹1,51,200 (A). Leaving out the General Reserve gives ₹1,32,200 (C). Sharing the revaluation profit in the new ratio (₹3,500) gives ₹1,46,500 (D).

questions.topic: Unit II: Reconstitution of a Partnership Firm
questions.question:
Read the following case and answer the question that follows.

P and Q are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3 : 2. On 1 April 2026 they admit R as a new partner, and the new profit-sharing ratio of P, Q and R is 2 : 1 : 1. On that date their balance sheet showed: Capitals — P ₹1,20,000 and Q ₹80,000; General Reserve ₹25,000; Building ₹1,50,000; Stock ₹60,000; Debtors ₹50,000 less Provision for doubtful debts ₹2,000. It was agreed that: (i) Building be appreciated by 10%; (ii) Stock be reduced by ₹6,000; (iii) Provision for doubtful debts be maintained at 5% of debtors; (iv) Outstanding rent of ₹1,500 be recorded; and (v) R brings ₹80,000 as capital and ₹20,000 as premium for goodwill, in cash.

Question: The balance of R's Capital Account after his admission will be:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹80,000
Why: R's Capital Account is credited only with the capital he brings. The premium of ₹20,000 belongs to the sacrificing partners: Cash A/c Dr. ₹20,000; To Premium for Goodwill A/c; then Premium for Goodwill A/c Dr.; To P's and Q's Capital A/cs. R has no share in the General Reserve or the revaluation profit, because both relate to the period before he joined.
Why not the others:
(A) ₹1,00,000 wrongly adds the premium to his capital.
(B) ₹81,750 wrongly gives him 1/4 of the revaluation profit.
(C) ₹75,000 wrongly debits him with his own share of goodwill.
Key point: Incoming partner's capital = only the capital brought in; past gains belong to the old partners.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question:
Which of the following are limitations of financial analysis?
(A) It ignores changes in the price level.
(B) It ignores qualitative factors such as the quality of management.
(C) Its results can be distorted by window dressing.
(D) It provides exact predictions of future results.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: Financial analysis is based on historical, monetary figures. It ignores inflation (A) and non-monetary factors such as management quality or labour relations (B), and its results can be distorted when accounts are made to look better than they are (C).
Why not the others: Statement (D) is false — analysis helps estimate trends but cannot exactly predict the future, because it is based on past data. Options (A), (B) and (C) all include (D).
Key point: Analysis is a tool for judgement, not a forecast.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: A company's shareholders' funds are ₹6,00,000 and its total assets are ₹10,00,000. Its proprietary ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.6 : 1
Formula: Proprietary ratio = Shareholders' funds ÷ Total assets
Step 1: ₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 = 0.6 : 1 (60% of the assets are financed by the owners)
Common mistake: Inverting the ratio gives 1.67 : 1 (B). Using borrowed funds (₹4,00,000) in the numerator gives 0.4 : 1 (C). Dividing shareholders' funds by debt gives 1.5 : 1 (D).
Key point: A higher proprietary ratio means greater long-term solvency.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: A company's profit after interest and tax is ₹1,20,000. Tax is ₹40,000 and interest on long-term debt is ₹20,000. Its interest coverage ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 9 times
Formula: Interest coverage ratio = Net profit before interest and tax ÷ Interest on long-term debt
Step 1: PBIT = ₹1,20,000 + ₹40,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹1,80,000
Step 2: Ratio = ₹1,80,000 ÷ ₹20,000 = 9 times
Common mistake: Using profit after tax gives 6 times (B). Using profit before tax (₹1,60,000) gives 8 times (C). Adding back only the interest (₹1,40,000) gives 7 times (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: During the year a company: issued equity shares of ₹2,00,000 at a premium of 10%; redeemed debentures of ₹1,00,000 at a premium of 5%; paid interest on debentures of ₹18,000; and paid dividend of ₹40,000. Net cash flow from financing activities is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹57,000 inflow
Step 1: Inflow — issue of shares including premium = ₹2,00,000 × 110% = ₹2,20,000
Step 2: Outflows — redemption of debentures including premium = ₹1,05,000; interest paid = ₹18,000; dividend paid = ₹40,000; total ₹1,63,000
Step 3: Net = ₹2,20,000 − ₹1,63,000 = ₹57,000 inflow
Common mistake: Ignoring the share premium gives ₹37,000 (A). Redeeming at par gives ₹62,000 (C). Treating interest paid as operating (correct only for financial companies) gives ₹75,000 (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Cash flow statement — classification and non-cash items
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II for a non-financial company:

List-I (Transaction)
(A) Proceeds from issue of equity shares
(B) Purchase of patents
(C) Cash paid to suppliers of goods
(D) Conversion of debentures into equity shares

List-II (Treatment in cash flow statement)
(I) Investing activity
(II) Financing activity
(III) Operating activity
(IV) Not shown, being a non-cash transaction

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why:
(A) Issuing shares changes the size of owners' capital → financing (II).
(B) Patents are long-term intangible assets → investing (I).
(C) Paying suppliers is part of the main revenue activity → operating (III).
(D) Converting debentures into shares involves no cash, so AS-3 excludes it from the statement → (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps investing and financing; (B) treats patents as operating; (D) puts payment to suppliers in the non-cash category.
Key point: Only actual cash flows appear; non-cash transactions are disclosed separately.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: Revenue from operations is ₹7,50,000, of which ₹1,50,000 is cash revenue. Trade receivables were ₹70,000 at the beginning of the year and ₹80,000 at the end. The trade receivables turnover ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8 times
Formula: Trade receivables turnover = Credit revenue from operations ÷ Average trade receivables
Step 1: Credit revenue = ₹7,50,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹6,00,000
Step 2: Average receivables = (₹70,000 + ₹80,000) ÷ 2 = ₹75,000
Step 3: Ratio = ₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹75,000 = 8 times
Common mistake: Using total revenue gives 10 times (A). Using closing receivables gives 7.5 times (B). Using opening receivables gives 8.57 times (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Tools of financial analysis — comparative statements
questions.question: Comparative financial statements show:
options: A) Each item as a percentage of a common base only
B) Figures of two or more periods side by side, with absolute and percentage changes
C) Only the ratios of the current year
D) Cash inflows and outflows classified by activity
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Figures of two or more periods side by side, with absolute and percentage changes
Why: A comparative statement places the figures of different years (or firms) side by side and shows the change in amount and in percentage. This reveals trends such as growth in revenue or a rise in expenses.
Why not the others:
(A) describes common-size statements.
(C) describes ratio analysis.
(D) describes the cash flow statement.
Key point: Comparative → change over time; common-size → structure within one period.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.sub_topic: Financial statements of a company — Schedule III headings
questions.question: As per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013, Goodwill is shown in the balance sheet under the head:
options: D) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible assets (sub-head: Intangible assets)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible assets (sub-head: Intangible assets)
Why: Under Non-current assets, Schedule III has the head 'Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible assets', with separate sub-heads for tangible assets (PPE) and intangible assets such as goodwill, patents, trademarks and software.
Why not the others:
(A) Goodwill is not realised within 12 months.
(B) Loans and advances are amounts lent or paid in advance.
(C) 'Other non-current assets' is for items not covered elsewhere, such as long-term trade receivables.
Key point: Goodwill → Non-current assets → Intangible assets.

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: From the following, calculate the gross profit ratio: Revenue from operations ₹5,00,000; Opening inventory ₹60,000; Purchases ₹3,40,000; Direct expenses ₹20,000; Closing inventory ₹70,000.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 30%
Formula: Cost of revenue from operations = Opening inventory + Purchases + Direct expenses − Closing inventory
Step 1: Cost = 60,000 + 3,40,000 + 20,000 − 70,000 = ₹3,50,000
Step 2: Gross profit = ₹5,00,000 − ₹3,50,000 = ₹1,50,000
Step 3: GP ratio = ₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹5,00,000 × 100 = 30%
Common mistake: Leaving out direct expenses gives 34% (A). 70% (C) is the cost-of-revenue ratio. Ignoring the opening inventory gives 42% (D).

questions.topic: Unit V: Analysis of Financial Statements
questions.question: Revenue from operations is ₹8,00,000 and gross profit is ₹2,40,000. Office, administration and selling expenses total ₹80,000. Interest on borrowings is ₹10,000, and there was a loss of ₹6,000 on the sale of machinery. The operating profit ratio is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 20%
Formula: Operating profit = Gross profit − Operating expenses (office, administration, selling, distribution). Non-operating items such as interest and loss on sale of assets are EXCLUDED.
Step 1: Operating profit = ₹2,40,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹1,60,000
Step 2: Operating profit ratio = ₹1,60,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000 × 100 = 20%
Common mistake: 30% (A) is the gross profit ratio. Deducting interest and the loss on sale (₹1,44,000) gives 18% (B). Deducting only the interest (₹1,50,000) gives 18.75% (D).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: A salesman's commission is calculated in cell C2 with the formula =IF(B2>=50000,B2*10%,B2*5%). If cell B2 contains 40000, the value shown in C2 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2000
Formula: =IF(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)
Step 1: Condition: is 40000 ≥ 50000? → FALSE
Step 2: So the value_if_false part applies: 40000 × 5% = 2000
Common mistake: Applying the 10% rate gives 4000 (A). Returning B2 itself gives 40000 (B). Assuming a false condition returns zero gives 0 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: An employee's gross salary of ₹50,000 consists of Basic pay ₹30,000, DA ₹12,000 and HRA ₹8,000. Provident Fund is deducted at 12% of (Basic + DA), and professional tax of ₹200 is also deducted. The net salary is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ₹44,760
Step 1: PF = 12% × (₹30,000 + ₹12,000) = ₹5,040
Step 2: Total deductions = ₹5,040 + ₹200 = ₹5,240
Step 3: Net salary = ₹50,000 − ₹5,240 = ₹44,760
Common mistake: Calculating PF on basic pay only (₹3,600) gives ₹46,200 (A). Calculating PF on gross salary (₹6,000) gives ₹43,800 (B). Forgetting the professional tax gives ₹44,960 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question:
Which of the following are features of an electronic spreadsheet?
(A) Formulas are recalculated automatically when a value changes.
(B) Data can be sorted and filtered.
(C) Data cannot be presented in the form of charts.
(D) Built-in functions such as SUM, IF and VLOOKUP are available.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: Automatic recalculation (A), sorting and filtering (B) and built-in functions (D) are core spreadsheet features that make it useful for accounting reports.
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — spreadsheets can turn data into column, bar, line and pie charts, which the syllabus covers under 'Graphs and Charts for Business Data'. Options (B), (C) and (D) all include (C).
Key point: Spreadsheet = calculation + data handling + presentation (charts).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question:
Arrange the following account heads from the broadest to the most detailed level, as in the hierarchy of a computerised accounting system:
(A) Ledger account 'Cash in Hand'
(B) Group 'Current Assets'
(C) Head 'Assets'
(D) Sub-group 'Cash and Cash Equivalents'
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Why: The chart of accounts is a hierarchy. Broad heads (Assets, Liabilities, Equity, Income, Expenses) are divided into groups, groups into sub-groups, and sub-groups into individual ledger accounts:
Assets (C) → Current Assets (B) → Cash and Cash Equivalents (D) → Cash in Hand (A)
Why not the others: (B) puts the group above the head; (C) puts the sub-group above the group; (D) is the reverse order (detailed to broad).
Key point: Head → group → sub-group → ledger account, each with a code that reflects its level.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Loan repayment schedule — equal principal instalments
questions.question: A loan of ₹2,00,000 at 10% p.a. is repaid in 4 equal annual principal instalments of ₹50,000, with interest on the outstanding balance paid at the end of each year. In a loan repayment schedule, the total payment in Year 2 is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ₹65,000
Given: Equal PRINCIPAL instalments (not equal total instalments); interest on the opening balance of each year.
Step 1: Balance at the start of Year 2 = ₹2,00,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹1,50,000
Step 2: Interest for Year 2 = 10% × ₹1,50,000 = ₹15,000
Step 3: Total payment = ₹50,000 + ₹15,000 = ₹65,000
Common mistake: Charging interest on the original loan gives ₹70,000 (B). Using the closing balance (₹1,00,000) gives ₹60,000 (C). ₹63,094 (D) is the equal PMT instalment, which applies only when the total instalments are equal.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.sub_topic: Graphs and charts for business data
questions.question: To show the share of each expense in a business's total monthly expenses, the most suitable spreadsheet chart is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Pie chart
Why: A pie chart shows how a whole (total expenses = 100%) is divided into parts, so each slice shows one expense's share at a glance.
Why not the others:
(A) A line chart shows a trend over time.
(C) A scatter chart shows the relationship between two variables.
(D) An area chart shows the volume of change over time.
Key point: Parts of a whole → pie; trend → line; comparison of categories → column/bar.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: In a computerised accounting system, a transaction is entered only once, and the ledger, trial balance and financial reports are prepared from it automatically. This feature is known as:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Automated processing
Why: In CAS, once a voucher is entered, the software posts it to the ledger accounts and updates the trial balance and reports without any further human effort. This speed and accuracy is the main advantage over manual accounting.
Why not the others:
(A) Codification assigns codes to accounts.
(B) An audit trail traces each entry to its source.
(D) Back-up is a copy of the data kept for safety.
Key point: Single entry of data → automatic posting and reports.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Error display)
(A) #DIV/0!
(B) #NAME?
(C) #VALUE!
(D) #####

List-II (Cause)
(I) Column is too narrow to display the value
(II) Formula divides by zero or by an empty cell
(III) Function or range name is not recognised
(IV) Wrong type of data used in a formula

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why:
(A) #DIV/0! — division by zero or a blank cell → (II).
(B) #NAME? — misspelt function or undefined name, e.g. =SUMM(A1:A5) → (III).
(C) #VALUE! — wrong data type, e.g. adding text to a number → (IV).
(D) ##### — the value is fine but the column is too narrow; widening the column fixes it → (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps #NAME? and #VALUE!; (B) swaps #DIV/0! and #####; (D) swaps #DIV/0! and #NAME?.
Key point: Learn each error code with its cause and its fix.

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: A machine costs ₹1,00,000, has a salvage value of ₹10,000 and a useful life of 5 years. The value returned by =DDB(100000,10000,5,1) for the first year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 40,000
Given: DDB (double-declining balance) charges depreciation at twice the straight-line rate on the opening book value.
Step 1: Straight-line rate = 1/5 = 20%; DDB rate = 2 × 20% = 40%
Step 2: Year 1 depreciation = 40% × ₹1,00,000 = ₹40,000 (salvage is not deducted from the cost; it only stops the book value from falling below ₹10,000)
Common mistake: 18,000 (A) is the SLN value (₹90,000 ÷ 5). 20,000 (B) is the cost ÷ life. Applying 40% to cost − salvage gives 36,000 (C).

questions.topic: Optional to Unit V: Computerised Accounting System
questions.question: A depreciation schedule is prepared in a spreadsheet for a machine costing ₹2,00,000, depreciated at 20% p.a. on the written-down value. The book value of the machine at the end of the third year is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ₹1,02,400
Given: WDV method — each year's depreciation is 20% of the OPENING book value.
Step 1: Year 1: depreciation ₹40,000 → book value ₹1,60,000
Step 2: Year 2: depreciation ₹32,000 → book value ₹1,28,000
Step 3: Year 3: depreciation ₹25,600 → book value ₹1,02,400 (i.e. ₹2,00,000 × 0.8³)
Common mistake: Using 20% of cost each year (straight line) gives ₹80,000 (A). Stopping after two years gives ₹1,28,000 (C). ₹97,600 (D) is the total depreciation over three years, not the book value.
